editorial.headline: Manual Instruments, Precision Work, and a Bali Registration Caveat
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 26511 covers manual measuring and testing instruments, nationally open to foreign investment but requiring careful Bali risk-scope verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 26511 is a manufacturing classification for manual measuring, checking, and testing equipment. Its scope is mechanical and practical: instruments used to measure, inspect, test, weigh, orient, meter, or support land measurement. The record includes examples such as measuring apparatus, thermometers, barometers, compasses, precision scales, mechanical therapy equipment, tape measures, water and gas meters, and land-measuring instruments. It also includes equipment accessories, which matters because the activity is not limited to a finished instrument alone; it reaches the supporting fittings that belong to that manual measurement and testing ecosystem.

For founders, the commercial signal is broad rather than niche. This is not framed as a scientific research service, a retail trade activity, or a digital platform category. It is the making of manual instruments and related equipment. The eligible business scales are also broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all listed as open. That means the classification can be used across a spectrum of operating sizes, from a small workshop-style manufacturing operation to a larger industrial producer, provided the declared activity stays inside the record’s stated manufacturing scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%, with the source stated as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national table treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full ceiling shown in the record. There is no lower national cap in the slim record, and there is no additional national threshold, licence, timeline, or capital figure supplied here, so none should be read into the classification.

Bali is the more careful part of the reading. The record does not say this activity is simply blocked in Bali; `l4_bali_blocked` is false. But it does mark the Bali status as `BLOCCATO_DIPENDE_SCOPE`, and the reason is exacting: “OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity.” The moratorium rule supplied in the record is also blunt: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. The honest conclusion is therefore not that Bali has a separate ownership percentage. It does not, in this record. The conclusion is that a PMA founder looking at Bali must verify the live OSS risk treatment for the exact declared activity, because the Bali issue turns on risk scope under the moratorium, not on a separate Bali foreign-share cap.
editorial.pullQuote: The Bali question is not a separate foreign-share percentage; it is whether the exact declared activity survives the province’s Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium in live OSS.
